# The Night The Coolroom Died

*(Or: A Cup Week Memoir, Written For Jonno, Who Is Not Here And Shouldn't Have Moved To London)*

---

Dear Jonno,

You saw my story. Then you sent me eleven messages, one of which was just the word "WHAT" in capitals, which honestly is the most effort you've put into anything since you moved. So here it is. The full thing. Written down. You're welcome. No more typing, no more voice notes you don't listen to, no more me explaining things while my hands are covered in stock.

Also I just finished a double so if the spelling's wrong, that's on the double, not on me.

Context, since you've clearly gone soft: this was Cup Day. Tuesday the 3rd of November. 140 covers booked, set menu, three courses, every single one of them cooked by us, in our kitchen, on a Tuesday, in Melbourne. And the reason I know every minute of it is that our coolroom compressor died in the night and by 6:40am the place was sitting at eleven degrees.

Eleven. Not "a bit warm." Eleven. The sort of number where you open the door and the food doesn't look rotten yet, it looks *confused*. Like it's considering its options.

Let me set the scene properly, because you would have absolutely lost your mind and I need you to understand that while reading this at 2am in your little London flat with your little flat white.

---

## 6:40am, and the maths starts immediately

Compressors don't die politely. There's no warning, no little noise, no "hey mate, think you might want to service me soon." It just goes. Somewhere between Monday night and Tuesday morning it went, and by the time I got in, the whole back of the house was warm and the stock was doing the thing where you don't look at it too directly.

The first thing you do is not panic. The second thing you do is call the fridge guy. The third thing you do is open every fridge in the building and start mentally triaging.

Wally from Coldline is a legend and Wally from Coldline could not come until Wednesday. Because the part was in Sydney. Sydney. On a Tuesday. In a country with actual roads and actual freight. So Wally said "mate, it's on its way," and I said "mate, I have 140 covers at lunch," and Wally said "yeah, that'll be right," and then I could hear him putting his phone down to go have a nice calm breakfast while my entire week fell over.

That's the industry, Jonno. That's the whole industry. It's just people saying "that'll be right" to each other while the actual problem sits in a loading dock in Mascot.

---

## The plan, which was basically "put everything in every fridge we could find"

So we moved everything. All of it. Into the two undercounters, the bar fridge, and — and this is the bit I'd genuinely never have believed if you hadn't seen it with your own eyes — half of Marta's walk-in next door.

Marta runs the cafe next door. Marta, who has never once in her life said no to us, who has fed us staff meals when we were dead, who once let us raid her freezer at 11pm for a bag of crumbed whiting that we did not pay for and did not feel guilty about. Marta opened her walk-in, said "half of it, not all of it," and went back to making her flat whites like a woman who has her shit together, which she does, and which I do not.

We lost about $1800 of stock. Mostly dairy, because dairy is the thing that goes first and goes hardest. The duck legs were a write-off. Just write them off, see them in the bin, don't think about it. That's how you survive service in a bistro kitchen. You do not think about it. You think about it at 11:30pm in the car park afterwards, and then you don't think about it again.

Raff's away this week, which means I was running it. So every dumb decision below was technically mine, which is why I'm telling you about them, because if you'd been here you'd have taken the wheel and done it properly and I'd have resented you for it.

---

## The beef shin and the milk crate trolley

This is the part where it becomes genuinely stupid, and I need you to appreciate that I am aware of how stupid it is.

Thirty kilos of beef shin. Needed to come down the laneway from the cold store because we had nowhere to put it and no cold room to put it in. So me and Benny — Benny who is 19, Benny who has never once complained about anything in his life — loaded it onto a milk crate trolley and pushed it down the laneway. In the rain.

One wheel fell off.

Not "a wheel squeaked." A wheel *fell off*. Fell off the trolley and rolled away down the laneway and I watched thirty kilos of beef shin get slowly dragged sideways into a puddle while Benny chased it, and honestly, if you had been standing there, you would have cried. You would have cried and said "this is the greatest night of my life" and meant it, because you were always the one who got louder the worse it got, and I mean that as a compliment. You fed off chaos. You were basically a bottle of champagne at a car fire.

London's made you soft, mate. You text me about meal deals now. I've seen it. You've got a little app. You go to pubs with a *reservation*. You'd have cried and I'd have had to hold your hand.

---

## The esky

Dishy Kev, god bless him, did something that day that should be taught in hospitality schools.

We had no ice. No ice because the compressor was dead and the ice machine lives in the coolroom. So Kev took the old esky — the ancient green one we've had since before the restaurant had a name — and filled it with ice from the servo down the road.

Fourteen bags.

He carried them in on his own. Fourteen bags of servo ice, up the laneway, in the rain, in the good shoes he definitely did not buy for work. And the servo guy — the servo guy looked at him and said, "you having a party?"

And Kev said, "yeah, we're having a party."

We were not having a party. We were having a Tuesday. But that's the thing about Kev, he never half-asses anything. The esky was the coldest thing in the building for the rest of the day. It had actual ice in it. It had *servo* ice. It was, functionally, the most beautiful object in that kitchen.

---

## Service: the panna cotta gets 86'd at 12:15

Right. Lunch. 140 covers. Set menu. Three courses.

And at 12:15pm I made the call. We had no panna cotta. So we 86'd it, and the dessert became "affogato with whatever."

With whatever. I want to be very clear that that was the actual announcement. I walked out to table 9 and said "we've had to kill the panna cotta, but we've got an affogato with whatever," and they said yes, and I thought, right, this is going well.

Then table 22 asked if they could have extra ice cream. And table 5 asked for the affogato with the *other* thing. And a table of four went "oh, that's actually better than the panna cotta would've been." Which — rude, but also correct.

We sold more desserts than we sold panna cotta in the last three weeks of October combined. The affogato with whatever was, and I will die on this hill, better than the panna cotta ever was. Nobody noticed. Nobody cares what was on the menu. They care that someone brought them something hot and cold and a bit boozy and told a joke about it.

Also: a lady on table 9 — different table 9 to the dessert table 9, don't worry — looked out the window at the laneway, where Benny and I were standing in the rain next to a trolley with no wheel, holding up thirty kilos of beef shin like a fitness meme, and asked if the beef was "free range from the laneway."

I said yes. I said yes, absolutely, free range, laneway-raised, grass-fed.

It was not. But she had a laugh and she had a great steak and she left a good tip, and I would do it again.

---

## The thing nobody tells you about bistro kitchens

They run on bar fridges and spite. That's it. That's the whole business model. If you take the temper out of a bistro kitchen — literally, if you take the *temperature* out — you don't get a crisis, you get a very tired staffroom and a hole in the wall where the profits were.

And then some bloke who owns the place leans in the doorway — our owner, Phil, lovely bloke, genuinely lovely — and says "just make it work mate," and goes back to his office.

"Just make it work mate" is not a plan. "Just make it work mate" is the hospitality version of "thought you'd ask someone else." But here's the thing, and I don't say this enough: we did make it work. Not just made it work — we had the best service of the year.

Everyone was locked in. Not locked-in-tired, not locked-in-suing-us-later locked in. Locked in like we'd all decided beforehand that Tuesday was *ours*. The whole crew. Nobody cracked, nobody went quiet, nobody hid in the dry store. We ran a 140-cover three-course lunch off a dead coolroom, half a walk-in next door, an esky full of servo ice and an affogato with whatever, and every single table got fed on time and nobody complained about anything except the rain.

That's not a sob story. That's just the job being good for once.

---

## The horse

I had a runner in the sweep called Ice Cold Lad and it came second last, which I think is the universe taking an extremely direct personal interest in me. One racer, Ice Cold Lad, and he's the one that suffers. That's the story of my November.

Wally called Wednesday and said the part was out of Sydney and installed it that afternoon like nothing had happened, which it hadn't, from his point of view. From mine it had cost a fortune and my spine still hurts from that trolley.

And then I owe Marta three weeks of staff meal in croissant credit, which means Marta has essentially bought my labour for November and is going to be owed a favour that can never be repaid, and honestly I've never been more comfortable in my life.

---

## Right, that's the story

That's the lot. Coolroom died, dinner became a party, we lost eighteen hundred bucks of dairy and I got to run my first full service, and I probably need to sleep for a week.

You're in London. You're doing whatever it is you're doing over there, and it's fine, and London's good for you, and I don't say that with any venom in my body at all. But you don't get to be far away during Cup Week. Nobody does. The whole city stands still for ten minutes and everybody's in a hat and it's basically the only thing we do as a country that isn't a bit embarrassing.

And you missed the ice. That's the thing you actually missed. Not the food, you'd have complained about the food. You missed the four servo guys and the trolley with no wheel and Kev heroically carrying fourteen bags of ice in the rain in his good shoes, and you would've stood in the middle of that kitchen filming it on your phone for the story, and then you'd have sent it to me with three crying-laughing emojis and the caption "THIS IS THE GREATEST NIGHT OF MY LIFE."

You'd of lost it, mate. Completely. And I would have loved every second of watching you lose it.

Anyway. It was the best service we did all year.

Come home ya flog. It's Cup Week. It's meant to be here.

— *Me*

---

*P.S. If you're showing this to anyone from London who thinks a broken fridge is a rough day, please remember: the ducks were never recovered and we don't talk about it.*
